title: Early pay stories: the quarter and the meatball
summary: As a young player he got shorted $0.25 by a booker and learned to reach at the table among old-timers.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Yeah, he was, you know what I mean, he don't get the credit that he really deserved. They gave more credit to fellas like Thomas Jefferson, than they gave to Rene. But you see, them old fellas and band leaders, they used to pull some deals off. I played with T-Boy Remy. And he took me on a job up to Raceland. I didn't know it was going to be a taxi dance. Yeah. I'm looking for a player that we have intermission. He said, what you want to stop for? I said, man, at least I got to go in the trailer, get a drink. Go ahead and come on by if we keep playing. Mm-hmm. And the job only paid $4. Mm-hmm. So fella picked us up in a truck, you know, and rode us to the ferry, Jackson Street. Mm-hmm. We caught the ferry and come over. He still hadn't paid me.
And we got on a Jackson Street car and we're coming.
He said, man, what about my money?
Oh, yeah, all right. And like he was going to get off at the next corner, and then he gave me my money, rolled up.

When I look at it, it was $3.75 instead of $4. That quarter meant a lot. My man, that's a fella who booked us. I said, man, if I'm a catcher, I'll break your name. Don't call me to book. That's for that quarter. And another time we was on a job, we went, I don't know who was playing, but I think Joe Rene was on that job. Bill Matthews. We went down the valley or a bureau somewhere down the line. Mm-hmm. Off the river. Those people had a big table spread out with food. But me, I'm a young fella with the band. All of them old timers reach and look like they got five arms coming off each body. When they got through reaching, there was one meatball left.

So the lady, these kids would come there, raise themselves, and we all didn't leave the little kid nothing. I said, that's all right. There's one meatball that they had, what you call, Dove and Spaghetti, chicken meatball. And a big piece of meatball. And a big piece of chunks of meat like that. And she said, that's right. Come here, son. She took me on the side to fill my plate up. She said, now here, you eat, you don't eat with them.
I said, I'm nice waiting instead of me grabbing like them.

No. They grabbing that one meatball left. And I'm surprised. If I wouldn't have reached for that, but I wouldn't have got that one meatball. So I come back. I was telling my brother Clarence about it. He said, look, next time you get out there, you reach. When they reach, you reach with both hands. See, because that's the way they're all. They'll eat up everything you install. Yeah. Yeah. But I learned a lot from those fellas, you know. Old Tom Copen, another bass player. I've been trying to think of him. I remember he was playing for a win on Corn Eye, a girl I went to school with, on Corn Eye between Russian Blade and Tartee. And my brother, man, he yelled, come on, let's go cut his head. Come on, let's go. He used to take me around. Yeah. Everybody hit me, but I got to cut his head, you know. So I learned one thing from him. He used to play some. He played that once, and I got it, and I started doing it more. He said, oh, that kid can play. Let him be letting me sit up and play it almost a whole night. He gave almost a whole night for him. Yeah, but man, he had that. I remember one time they was rehearsing at the Tulane Hall, a WPA band. And he used to try to get me to join a WPA band. I said, no, man, I'm working on nightclubs. I ain't thinking about it. But WPA band, all them fellas, they wasn't working on nightclubs. They got a job maybe once every month or maybe twice a month, one deal like that. Yeah, I'm working regular. So I happened to come up there when we went on it, and Sun Johnson and about three or four of us were just playing together. And I'm on, I forgot whose bass it was. It must have been Albert Glennie. I think he was in his bass or somebody's bass that playing. Boy, that band conductor come in and he heard us there. He jumped all over them. By me being in that playing, which I just said, good day. I turned around, walked around. And he wanted to find out who I was. He invited me to join a dude. I couldn't be, you know what I mean? I couldn't be with music. It's always something happy to me. The main thing while I still stick with it, I'm glad to get out there and make people smile, make people laugh, you know? And when I see an audience, some ignorant person in it, like he come over there, I can't even think of his name, which it don't mean nothing to me. Who was the conductor of the WPA band?
